overview: This file consists of a State Department cross-reference note and the supplemental portion of a report prepared at the American Consulate in Yokohama by Vice Consul Hayward G. Hill, completed May 2 and mailed May 7, 1932, in response to a Department instruction concerning manning, wages, and subsistence allowances aboard Japanese vessels trading with the United States. The surviving supplement describes the origins and functions of the Kaiji Kyodokwai marine labor organization; reproduces its minimum pay agreements for officers, wireless operators, and crews; compares company wages, navigation allowances, bonuses, and retirement benefits; and translates Japanese statutory requirements for licensed officers. A revised index and a confidential source sheet show that the report combined published Japanese materials with interviews and information obtained through consular employees and their shipping-industry contacts.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note for Hill's report on Japanese ship's officers
subfiles.about: The sheet directs readers to the supplemental report and highlights its conclusion about the limited scope of Japanese vessel-manning law.
subfiles.summary: The filing note identifies a May 2, 1932 report from Hill at Yokohama concerning Japanese law on ship's officers. It emphasizes that, apart from the requirements quoted on report pages 30–31, Japanese law prescribed no other vessel-manning scales.

subfiles.title: Title and approval sheet for the supplemental report
subfiles.about: The cover identifies the supplemental report on personnel and compensation aboard Japanese vessels trading with the United States.
subfiles.summary: This sheet records that Hill prepared the report at the American Consulate in Yokohama in compliance with the Department's instruction of October 8, 1931. It gives May 2, 1932 as the completion date, May 7 as the mailing date, and notes its approval by American Consul Charles L. De Vault.

subfiles.title: Revised index to the combined shipping-labor report
subfiles.about: The index outlines both the previously submitted report and its new supplemental sections.
subfiles.summary: The index lists the original report's company-by-company treatment of vessels, manning, wages, allowances, and financial standing. It then identifies supplemental material on the Kaiji Kyodokwai, minimum wage agreements, company practices, navigation and retirement allowances, Japanese officer law, and confidential sources.

subfiles.title: Supplemental report on Japanese seamen, officers, wages, and maritime law
subfiles.about: The report supplements an earlier study with union agreements, company compensation data, and a translation of Japanese law governing ship's officers.
subfiles.summary: Hill explains that the new pages were intended to be inserted into the report submitted in April 1932. The supplement traces the government-directed formation of the Kaiji Kyodokwai and reproduces its minimum salary and wage agreements for wireless operators, deck and engineering officers, crewmen, and apprentices. It compares those standards with the wages, voyage allowances, annual bonuses, and retirement benefits paid by the Nippon Yusen Kaisha, Osaka Shosen Kaisha, and other lines, observing that some actual allowances fell well below Kaiji Kyodokwai rates. The closing section translates statutory licensing and complement requirements for officers and concludes that Japanese law imposed no other vessel-manning scales.

subfiles.title: Confidential source-of-information sheet
subfiles.about: The sheet identifies the documentary, interview, and personal sources used for each part of the combined report.
subfiles.summary: Sources included consular bills of health, interviews with steamship officials, information gathered by Vice Consul Benninghoff, and an interview with Osaka Shosen Kaisha manager Makino. Ichiro Suzuki of the Kobe consulate obtained the Kaiji Kyodokwai pamphlet and secured additional wage information through friends in the local shipping business; other portions rested on translated publications or the reporting officer's opinions.

interest: The file offers unusually detailed quantitative evidence about the hierarchy of pay in Japan's interwar merchant marine, extending from masters and engineers to apprentices and mess attendants. Particularly revealing is the comparison between Kaiji Kyodokwai standards and the substantially lower navigation allowances actually paid by some companies, which led Hill to question the union's enforcement power. The translated legal provisions distinguish formal state regulation of licensed officers from privately negotiated wage and manning practices, while the confidential source sheet exposes the personal and institutional networks through which American consular officers gathered commercial and labor information.
